justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a relatively stable underlying trend with a modest upward drift across horizons. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 94.1 is anchored heavily to the most recent observed value, with only minimal expected movement given typical short-term persistence. At the one-week horizon, the slight increase to 94.3 reflects a small continuation of whatever directional momentum was present in recent data, though the adjustment is modest because short-term trends tend to be weak predictors beyond a day or two. The one-month estimate of 94.8 extends this gentle drift further, incorporating a longer-run mean or trend component that pulls the forecast modestly higher, while still remaining close to current levels given the mean-reverting tendencies common in many financial or economic series.

The confidence interval widths widen appropriately as the horizon extends, reflecting the compounding of uncertainty over time. At one day, the 90% interval spans roughly 3.2 units, consistent with typical daily volatility being relatively contained. By one week, the interval expands to about 5.6 units, capturing the accumulation of day-to-day uncertainty over five trading or calendar days. At one month, the interval stretches to roughly 11.5 units, reflecting that over approximately 20–30 periods, small daily shocks can compound substantially. The widening follows a pattern broadly consistent with a square-root-of-time scaling, though not perfectly so, as some structural uncertainty also enters at longer horizons.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside these intervals include sudden macroeconomic shocks, policy announcements, or geopolitical events that create discontinuous jumps in the underlying series. Liquidity crises or sharp sentiment shifts could drive the value well below 92.5 even within a single day. On the upside, an unexpected positive catalyst — a strong data release, a policy easing, or a resolution of an existing risk — could push above 95.7 in the near term. At the one-month horizon, the tails are particularly exposed to regime changes, such as a sustained shift in volatility, a structural break in trend, or correlated macro developments that invalidate the stationarity assumptions embedded in the forecast. These fat-tail events are by definition underrepresented in interval estimates that assume relatively normal error distributions.
